Proposals for race- and nationality-based immigration quotas remain marginalized in contemporary debate due to their incompatibility with U.S. legal standards, ethical norms, and the principles of equality enshrined in law.   • The Supposed Benefit: By restricting immigration from these "less desirable" groups, proponents argued they were practicing a form of "national eugenics." The benefit was framed as improving the overall quality and health of the American population by preventing "racial degradation."

3. Economic and Labor Protectionism

  • The Argument: Following waves of industrialization and the labor movements of the late 19th century, there was significant fear among labor unions and others that a large influx of immigrants would drive down wages and take jobs from native-born American workers. This economic anxiety was often racially tinged, with new immigrant groups being characterized as willing to work for "starvation wages" and used as strikebreakers.
  • The Supposed Benefit: Quotas were seen as a way to protect the economic interests of the existing (predominantly white) workforce. By severely limiting the labor supply from certain regions, the policy aimed to stabilize or increase wages and reduce competition for jobs.
